7000:
To gormandize means to eat greedily and excessively — to stuff yourself with food in a way that shows very little self-control or restraint. When someone gormandizes, they don't eat because they are simply hungry. They eat far beyond what they need, driven by a powerful, almost animal-like desire for food.

Think of someone sitting at a holiday feast who, long after everyone else has stopped, keeps piling food onto their plate, shoveling it in rapidly, barely pausing to breathe, going back for thirds and fourths — that person is gormandizing.
The Full Picture — What the Word Really Captures

The word carries two layers that often appear together:

1. The quantity: The person is eating a large amount — far more than is normal or necessary.

2. The manner: The eating is done greedily — with urgency, without elegance, and without much thought for others at the table.

It is not just "eating a lot." You could eat a lot slowly, gracefully, and politely. That would not be gormandizing. Gormandizing suggests something almost uncontrolled about the eating — a surrender to appetite. The person is governed by their hunger rather than governing it.

This word is mildly judgmental. When you use it to describe someone, you are not being completely neutral — you are painting a picture of someone who is being a little gluttonous, a little undignified around food. It is not a vicious insult, but it is not a compliment either. It sits somewhere between gentle mockery and mild disapproval.

That said, it can also be used humorously and affectionately — someone might say "we spent the whole evening gormandizing" about themselves with a laugh, acknowledging that they went overboard but enjoyed every second of it.

• "The children gormandized their way through the entire pizza, leaving nothing for the adults."
  • "He spent the holidays gormandizing without guilt, reasoning that January was made for diets."
  • "She watched in mild horror as her guests gormandized through three courses in under twenty minutes."
  • "Every summer, we'd travel to the coast and simply gormandize on fresh seafood for a week."

Notice how in each case, there is a sense of excess, urgency, or indulgence — not calm, measured eating.

It is worth clearing up a possible confusion. A gourmet is someone who has refined, sophisticated taste in food — they care deeply about quality. A gourmand is someone who loves food and eats a lot of it, but is still associated with an appreciation of good food. Gormandizing, however, strips away most of the sophistication. When someone gormandizes, the focus is on the greed and excess, not on appreciation or taste. You can gormandize on cheap, ordinary food just as easily as on fine cuisine.

In short: a gourmet savors. A gormandizer devours.

• Gormandizer (noun) — a person who gormandizes; a greedy eater.
  • Gormandizing (present participle / adjective) — "his gormandizing habits caught up with him."
  • Gormandizement (noun, rare) — the act of gormandizing.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

To gormandize = to eat greedily and excessively, with more appetite than restraint.

If you can picture someone with food on their chin, plate overflowing, eating fast and asking for more — that's gormandizing.
7001:
Gormless means stupidly unaware, blank, and lacking any common sense or mental sharpness. It describes a person who just doesn't "get it" — someone who stares blankly, understands things slowly, and seems to have no alertness or initiative in their mind whatsoever.

Think of it this way: imagine someone standing in front of you while you explain something simple. Their mouth is slightly open. Their eyes are glazed over. They blink. They clearly have no idea what's happening. That person, in that moment, is being completely gormless.
What Makes It Special — The Nuances

"Gormless" is not just a synonym for "stupid." It has a very specific flavour. It combines three things at once:

1. A lack of intelligence or understanding.
A gormless person is slow to grasp things. They miss what's obvious to everyone else.

2. A lack of alertness and awareness.
They seem mentally absent — as if the lights are on, but nobody is home. There's a vacancy to them. This is perhaps the most important quality of the word. A gormless person doesn't just fail to understand something; they don't even seem to notice that there's something to understand.

3. A lack of initiative and common sense.
They won't take sensible action, not because they're lazy, but because they simply can't figure out what sensible action even looks like.

The word often has a visual quality to it. A "gormless expression" or a "gormless look" is a very common phrase — it describes that blank, vacant, slightly open-mouthed face that signals absolutely nothing is going on inside.

• It is a British English word, used widely in the UK and in other places influenced by British culture (Australia, parts of Canada, etc.). If you use it in American English, people may not recognise it.
  • It is informal and colloquial. You would not use it in a formal essay or a business report. It belongs in everyday conversation.
  • It is mildly insulting, but not harshly so. It sits in the zone of affectionate exasperation rather than genuine contempt. A parent might call their teenager gormless. Friends might call each other gormless while laughing. A boss, however, would rarely say it to an employee without it being offensive.
  • It is often used with some humour. The word itself has a slightly comic sound to it, and the situations it describes — someone standing there utterly baffled by something simple — are often described with a smirk rather than real anger.

• "He just stood there with a gormless expression, staring at the broken printer as if he'd never seen one before."

— He looked blank and helpless, with no idea what to do.

  • "Don't be so gormless — can't you see she needs help carrying those bags?"

— Stop being oblivious and use some common sense.

  • "I've never met someone so gormless in my life. I had to explain the same thing four times, and he still looked confused."

— The person is frustratingly slow and vacant.

  • "She gave him a gormless smile and said, 'Sorry, what were we talking about?'"

— Her smile was vacant and uncomprehending.

  • "He wandered into the meeting late, looked around with that gormless look of his, and sat in the wrong seat."

— He was blissfully unaware and clueless about his surroundings.

On a scale of mild to very harsh, gormless sits on the milder side. It is more likely to make someone roll their eyes than genuinely wound them. It suggests someone is a bit hopeless and dim, but it doesn't attack their character or morals — only their wits. That said, calling someone gormless to their face, especially in a professional setting, would still be considered rude.

These words share territory with "gormless," but each has slightly different shades:

  • Clueless — unaware of what's going on (very close to gormless, but less specifically British and lacks the "vacant stare" quality)
  • Dim or dim-witted — not intelligent (focuses more on low intelligence, less on blankness)
  • Obtuse — slow to understand (more formal; focuses on stubbornness in not understanding)
  • Vacant — empty-headed and expressionless (captures the "blank look" part of gormless very well)
  • Witless — lacking sense or intelligence (similar, but sounds more old-fashioned)
  • Dopey — slow and silly (more playful and cartoon-like than gormless)

• Sharp — mentally quick and alert
  • Astute — clever at noticing and understanding things
  • Bright — intelligent
  • Shrewd — having good, practical judgment

If you need to remember just one thing: gormless = stupidly blank and clueless, in a slightly helpless, vacant way. It's the word for someone who stares at you as if you've just spoken in a language from another planet — even when you've said something perfectly simple.
7002:
Gory describes something that involves a large amount of blood, brutal violence, or the disturbing, graphic physical aftermath of injury or death. When you call something gory, you are saying it is not just violent — it is visually and viscerally graphic. The blood, wounds, and physical damage are prominently on display, often in a way that is shocking or unsettling.

Think of it this way: a punch in a film is violent. But if that punch splits someone's face open and blood pours everywhere, the scene becomes gory. The key ingredient is always that graphic, blood-soaked, flesh-and-wounds quality.

Gory works in two distinct ways in English:

1. Literally — describing actual blood and physical violence

This is the primary and most common use. Something is described as gory when it shows or involves real (or depicted) blood, wounds, death, or bodily harm in a graphic way.

  • "The horror film was so gory that some viewers walked out."
  • "The surgeon described the gory wound in detail."
  • "The battlefield photographs were too gory to be published in the newspaper."
  • "It was a gory accident — there was blood everywhere."

2. Figuratively — describing disturbing or unpleasant details of any situation

Over time, "gory" extended beyond physical violence. People began using it to mean disturbingly detailed or uncomfortably specific about any unpleasant situation, even one with no blood at all. This use is informal and very common in everyday conversation.

  • "I don't need to know the gory details of their divorce." (No blood — just messy, uncomfortable information.)
  • "She gave us every gory detail of how the business failed."

In this figurative sense, "gory" signals: "This is more than I wanted to know. It's unsettlingly specific and unpleasant."

Gory is a strong word. It is not used for mild violence or a small amount of blood. It implies something noticeably, even excessively, graphic. If someone describes a film as gory, you understand immediately that it features serious, stomach-turning violence — not just action. The word carries a sense of excess and shock.

It helps to understand what separates "gory" from similar words:

  • Violent is broader. Something can be violent (a loud argument, a forceful push) with no blood or graphic imagery at all. Gory always involves graphic physical content.
  • Scary or creepy are about fear and atmosphere. Something can be terrifying without a drop of blood. Gory is specifically about the visual, bloody, physical nature of something.
  • Gruesome is the closest synonym. Gruesome and gory are nearly identical in meaning and can usually replace each other. However, gruesome can lean slightly more toward disgust and horror, while gory emphasizes the blood-soaked, graphic quality specifically.
The Most Important Phrase to Know: "Gory Details"

The phrase "gory details" is so common in English that it deserves special attention. It means the specific, graphic, or uncomfortable particulars of something — the parts that are hard to hear or unpleasant to picture.

It is used in two ways:

  • Literally: "The detective described the gory details of the crime scene." (Actual graphic, bloody details.)
  • Figuratively: "Tell me everything — spare me none of the gory details." (Used humorously or dramatically to mean: tell me all of it, even the uncomfortable parts.)

You will hear this phrase constantly in everyday English, so recognizing it is very useful.
The Feeling Gory Gives the Reader or Listener

When a writer or speaker uses the word "gory," they are doing two things at once: describing graphic content and signaling a reaction to it. The word itself carries a slight tone of being shocked, disturbed, or even a little disgusted. It is rarely neutral. Using "gory" tells your audience: "This was not pretty. This was raw and graphic."

Gory = graphic, bloody, and disturbing in a way that shows the physical brutality of violence or injury — and by extension, disturbingly detailed about any unpleasant situation. It is always a strong word, always signals something unsettling, and is most famously used in the phrase "gory details."
7003:
When someone says something is "the gospel truth," they mean it is absolutely, completely, and without any doubt true. Not probably true. Not mostly true. 100% true — with zero room for questioning.

It is used to make a very strong statement about something being real and accurate, especially when the speaker wants to convince someone who might be skeptical or disbelieving.

Think of it this way: If a friend tells you something unbelievable and you raise an eyebrow, they might say — "I swear, that's the gospel truth!" — meaning: "Stop doubting me. Every single word of it is true."

To understand this idiom deeply, you need to understand the word "gospel" first.

The word gospel comes from the Old English word "gōdspel," which literally means "good news." In Christianity, the Gospels are the four sacred books at the beginning of the New Testament in the Bible — the books of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. These books describe the life, teachings, and actions of Jesus Christ.

For Christians, the Gospels were not just stories — they were considered the word of God. They were sacred, divine, and absolutely, unquestionably true. There was no higher authority. No more reliable source. No more trustworthy text in existence.

So when people began comparing something to "gospel truth," they were essentially saying: "This is as true as the word of God itself." That is the highest level of certainty a person could claim in a deeply religious society.

Over time, even as the expression moved away from strictly religious settings, it kept its powerful meaning — something completely and undeniably true.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The idiom is almost always used with the word "the" in front of it. You say "the gospel truth," not just "gospel truth" on its own (though you might occasionally hear it without "the" in very casual speech).

Here are some natural examples:

  • "I didn't touch your phone. That's the gospel truth."
  • "Everything she told you about that night is the gospel truth."
  • "He takes everything that man says as the gospel truth, even when it makes no sense."
  • "I'm telling you the gospel truth — I have never been to that city in my life."
  • "The report is the gospel truth; every number was verified three times."

Notice something across these examples: the idiom appears in situations where someone's honesty is being questioned or where the speaker feels the need to emphasize sincerity. It is a way of saying, "You can trust this completely."
A Closely Related Usage — "Take as Gospel"

You will also frequently see a shorter version of this idea: "take something as gospel" (sometimes "take it as gospel").

This means to accept something as completely true without questioning it at all — sometimes even when you perhaps shouldn't be so trusting.

For example:

  • "Don't take everything you read online as gospel."
  • "The students took the professor's words as gospel."

Here, the meaning carries a slight warning — it implies that the person is accepting something too blindly, with too much trust. So "take as gospel" can be either neutral or mildly critical depending on context.
The Tone and Feel of the Idiom

1. It is emphatic.
This idiom is used when you want to stress the truth of something. It adds emotional weight. It is stronger than just saying "I'm telling the truth" or "That's correct."

2. It has a slightly old-fashioned or traditional flavor.
It is not a modern slang term. It has been used in English for hundreds of years, and it carries a sense of heritage and gravity. You'll hear it a lot in literature, older films, and everyday speech — particularly in American Southern English and British English, where it remains very common.

3. It can be used seriously or with light humor.
Most of the time, people use it sincerely to insist something is true. But sometimes, it can be used humorously or sarcastically — for example, if someone is exaggerating or being dramatic, a listener might say with a smirk, "Oh yes, I'm sure that's the gospel truth." — meaning the opposite: "I don't believe a word of it."

4. It is informal.
You would not typically use this in formal academic writing. It fits naturally in conversation, storytelling, and informal writing.
Why People Use This Idiom (The Psychology Behind It)

When someone invokes "the gospel truth," they are doing something very specific — they are borrowing the authority of something universally trusted to back up their own words. This is why the phrase is so effective. The Gospels carried the highest possible authority in Western culture for centuries. By connecting your statement to that level of certainty, you are signaling: "My words deserve the same level of trust."

It also shows desperation to be believed. People don't usually say "that's the gospel truth" about everyday, uncontroversial things. They say it when they fear disbelief — when the thing they are saying sounds surprising, shocking, or hard to accept.

A few important clarifications:

  • It does not mean something is a religious truth. You don't have to be Christian to use it or hear it — it has long since become a general expression in everyday secular life.
  • It is not a mild expression. Calling something "the gospel truth" is a strong, emphatic claim. Using it for small, trivial things can sound odd or overdramatic.
  • It is not the same as "partial truth" or "mostly accurate." Gospel truth means the whole, complete, uncorrupted truth.

These expressions share a similar spirit:

  • "The honest truth" — emphasizes sincerity; slightly softer than gospel truth.
  • "The plain truth" or "the naked truth" — the truth without any decoration or hiding; blunt and raw.
  • "Swear on my life / mother's grave" — a personal oath used to emphasize one is not lying.
  • "Cross my heart" — a childhood promise gesture meaning "I am being completely truthful."
  • "Straight from the horse's mouth" — information coming directly from the original, most reliable source.

ConceptDetail

"The gospel truth" means something that is completely and absolutely true, with no doubt whatsoever. It comes from the Christian Gospels, which were considered the perfect, divine word of God — the highest possible standard of truth. People use this idiom when they strongly want to assert that something is true, especially when they feel they might not be believed. It can also appear as "take as gospel," meaning to accept something without any questioning — sometimes too blindly. The idiom is emphatic, slightly old-fashioned in flavor, informal in register, and is a timeless fixture of the English language.
7004:
When you call something gossamer, you are saying it is extremely thin, light, and delicate — so fine that it is nearly see-through, and so weightless that it seems like it could float away or vanish at any moment.

Think of a spider's web in the early morning, still wet with dew, catching the light. It is there, you can see it, but it feels like it barely exists in the physical world. It has almost no weight. It is fragile beyond measure. It is beautiful precisely because it is so impossibly fine. That is the perfect gossamer image.
What It Really Means — Layer by Layer

The adjective has two layers that work together: physical thinness and a feeling of dreamlike delicacy.

The physical layer is straightforward. Something gossamer is:

  • Extremely thin — like the finest fabric imaginable, or a single thread of silk
  • Nearly transparent or see-through
  • Weightless, or as close to it as a physical thing can be

The emotional/sensory layer is what makes the word special. Gossamer doesn't just mean thin. It carries a feeling of ethereal, almost unreal beauty. Something gossamer feels like it belongs to a dream, or to fairy tales, or to the magical in-between hour of early morning. It is not just delicate — it is breathtakingly delicate.

This combination — physical thinness + dreamlike beauty — is what separates gossamer from plain words like "thin" or "light."

Fabrics and clothing — This is probably the most common use. A gossamer veil, a gossamer gown, gossamer curtains. You are picturing the most delicate, sheer, barely-there fabric — fabric you can almost see straight through, that floats rather than falls.

Nature — Gossamer wings on a dragonfly or a fairy. Gossamer mist hovering just above a lake at dawn. A gossamer spider's web stretched between two branches.

Metaphorical use — This is where the word gets even more interesting. Writers use "gossamer" to describe non-physical things that feel fragile, fleeting, or barely-there:

  • A gossamer hope — a hope so fragile it might break if you look at it too hard
  • A gossamer memory — a memory so faint and delicate it could dissolve at any moment
  • A gossamer connection between two people — a bond that is beautiful but thin and easily broken

In metaphorical use, the word always carries that same core idea: beautiful, but barely holding together; present, but almost not.

This is important: gossamer is almost always a positive or neutral word. It is not an insult. When you describe something as gossamer, you are usually expressing wonder and admiration at how impossibly fine and beautiful it is.

Compare: calling a fabric "flimsy" suggests it is cheaply made and disappointing. Calling it "gossamer" suggests it is achingly beautiful in its delicacy. Same physical thinness, completely different emotional color.

The only time gossamer tilts slightly negative is in the metaphorical sense — a "gossamer promise" or "gossamer plan" might hint that something is too insubstantial to be trusted. But even then, it is more wistful than critical.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Sheer — means see-through, but has no particular sense of beauty or weightlessness. A sheer cliff face is sheer. Nothing gossamer about it.
  • Delicate — means fragile and fine, but doesn't carry the sense of being nearly invisible or weightless.
  • Filmy — similar to gossamer but more neutral and less poetic. A camera lens can be filmy. You wouldn't call it gossamer.
  • Diaphanous — this one is very close to gossamer, almost a synonym, and also means light and translucent. But gossamer is softer and more evocative, while diaphanous is more clinical and literal.

Gossamer occupies a unique spot because it insists on all three qualities at once: thinness, near-transparency, and an almost magical lightness — wrapped in a feeling of fragile beauty.

If you see the word "gossamer" in a sentence, ask yourself: What is being described as impossibly thin, light, and beautiful — almost too delicate to exist?

That is your gossamer thing.

She wore a gossamer shawl that seemed to be made of nothing but light and air.
The gossamer threads of the web trembled in the breeze.
Their relationship was built on gossamer trust — beautiful, but easily torn.

In each case, the word is doing the same job: making you feel the fragile, ethereal, dreamlike quality of something that is barely-there — and all the more beautiful for it.
7005:
Imagine you're walking through a garden on a quiet autumn morning. You look at the grass, the bushes, and the low branches — and you notice something almost magical: thin, silvery, almost invisible threads draped across everything. They are so fine and so light that they seem to barely exist. They shimmer when the light catches them. One breath of wind and they tremble or float away. These delicate threads, spun by tiny spiders and left behind on vegetation or drifting freely through the air, are called gossamer.

That is the original and most precise meaning of the noun: the fine, silky threads produced by small spiders, which are often seen floating in the air or resting on grass and plants, particularly in early morning or in autumn.

Understanding the word fully means understanding what makes gossamer so special. It is not just "a spider thread." The word carries a very specific combination of qualities:

  • Extreme delicacy — it is about as thin as something can possibly be while still being visible
  • Lightness — it has almost no weight at all
  • Near-transparency — it is so fine you can see right through it; it only becomes visible when light catches it at the right angle
  • Fragility — the slightest touch or movement can disturb or destroy it

These four qualities together are the soul of the word.

Because gossamer (the spider thread) is so famously thin, light, and transparent, the word expanded over time to describe any material or substance that shares those qualities — whether or not it involves spiders at all.

So in everyday use, gossamer as a noun can also refer to any extremely fine, light, and sheer fabric or filmy material. Think of the thinnest, most transparent silk you can imagine — so sheer it looks like it could dissolve into air. That kind of material can be called gossamer.

In this sense, it simply means: something material, yet barely there.

A useful way to anchor this word in your memory is to think of it as sitting at the very far end of a scale of thickness and weight — right at the edge of existing at all. If you imagine a scale from "heavy and solid" to "barely there," gossamer lives at the extreme "barely there" end, but it is still real and physical. It is not nothing — it is just almost nothing.

This is what separates it from words like "thin" or "light." Those are general. Gossamer is specific — it names a quality of such extreme, almost impossible delicacy that it feels closer to air than to matter.

You will encounter this noun most often in two situations:

1. In its literal, natural sense — referring to those floating spider threads, especially in descriptions of nature, seasons, or the outdoors. Writers describing autumn mornings, dewy fields, or quiet forests often use it.

2. As a transferred noun for fabric or material — describing something like ultra-fine silk, a bridal veil, a sheer curtain, or a delicate lace, where the point is to convey its near-weightless, transparent, fragile quality.

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

Gossamer is the fine, almost weightless, near-transparent silky thread spun by small spiders — and, by extension, any material that shares that same quality of extreme thinness, lightness, and delicacy.
What It Feels Like to Use the Word

When you call something gossamer, you are saying more than just "it is thin." You are evoking a feeling — a sense of something so fragile and light that it belongs more to the air than to the earth. It is a word that carries beauty and fragility in equal measure. Using it adds a sense of wonder and delicacy that a plain word like "thin" or "fine" simply cannot deliver.
7006:
Gossip is talk or information about other people's personal lives — especially when that talk happens behind those people's backs, often involves unverified or private details, and is shared mainly out of curiosity, entertainment, or social bonding rather than any serious purpose.

Think of it this way: when two people lean in and whisper, "Did you hear what happened to Meena's marriage?" — that conversation, and the information exchanged in it, is gossip.

Gossip almost always involves:

Other people — not the people talking, but a third party (someone who is absent from the conversation). This "behind the back" quality is central to gossip.

Personal or private matters — things like relationships, affairs, secrets, failures, scandals, financial troubles, embarrassing incidents, or anything that touches a person's private life.

Unverified or uncertain information — gossip is often rumour-based. It may be partly true, exaggerated, completely false, or a mix. Even when it turns out to be true, it was typically spread without confirmation. This is why gossip is considered unreliable.

A casual, informal register — gossip is not a formal report or a news broadcast. It travels through conversation, whispers, text messages, and informal social channels.

The word gossip as a noun carries two distinct but related meanings:

1. The Talk Itself (the more common meaning today)

This refers to the content — the stories, rumours, whispered information, and chatter about people's personal lives.

"The office was full of gossip after the manager suddenly resigned."

"She had no interest in celebrity gossip."

"I heard some gossip about the neighbours, but I'm not sure how much of it is true."

Here, gossip is an uncountable noun (like water or music) — you don't say "a gossip" or "three gossips" when referring to the talk itself. You say some gossip, a piece of gossip, a lot of gossip.

2. A Person Who Gossips (an older but still used meaning)

A gossip can also refer to a person — specifically, someone who habitually talks about other people's private business and spreads rumours. This usage implies criticism; calling someone "a gossip" is not a compliment.

"Don't tell her anything personal — she's a terrible gossip."

"The whole neighbourhood knew because one of the biggest gossips on the street had overheard the argument."

Here, gossip is a countable noun — a gossip, that gossip, two gossips.
What Makes Something "Gossip" and Not Just Ordinary Conversation?

This is a genuinely important and subtle distinction. Not all talk about other people is gossip. The key factors that push conversation into gossip territory are:

1. The absent subject — You're talking about someone who is not present and cannot speak for themselves or correct the record.

2. Private or personal content — The topic concerns someone's personal life, not their public role. Discussing a politician's voting record is not gossip. Whispering about that politician's secret affair is.

3. The informational status is uncertain — The information hasn't been verified. It was heard from someone, who heard it from someone else. There is a chain of transmission and, at each link, details can get distorted.

4. The motive is social, not practical — Gossip is shared for entertainment, to bond with the listener, to express disapproval of someone, to feel superior, or simply because it is interesting — not because the listener urgently needs to know for their own safety or benefit.

5. The subject would likely object — If the person being discussed would feel uncomfortable or violated knowing that this conversation was happening, it's probably gossip. Gossip thrives on secrecy and the exclusion of its subject.
The Tone of Gossip: Is It Always Negative?

Not always, but it skews negative. Here's the full range:

Negative gossip (the most common) involves criticism, scandal, or the exposure of failures and misfortunes. "Apparently Rohan lost all his money in a bad investment and his wife is furious."

Neutral gossip is just the informal sharing of news about someone's life. "Did you know Priya is moving to London next month?" This sits at the border between gossip and simple news-sharing.

Positive gossip (sometimes called flattery gossip) spreads complimentary information. "I heard Arjun got a huge promotion — apparently the CEO personally requested him." Even this can feel like gossip if the person didn't announce it themselves.

The reason gossip is generally seen as negative in moral and social terms — even when the content isn't — is because it involves discussing someone who cannot respond, potentially with incomplete or distorted information, which can damage reputations and betray trust.

Gossip is not simply a bad habit — it is a deeply human and universal social phenomenon that exists in every culture. Researchers who study social behaviour note that it serves several real social functions:

  • Bonding: Sharing gossip creates intimacy between the people sharing it. The act of "telling you something I shouldn't" is a form of trust.
  • Social norm enforcement: Gossip often targets people who have violated group norms (cheated on a partner, behaved dishonestly, etc.). Spreading that information is an informal way of punishing rule-breaking and warning others.
  • Information gathering: People learn about the social world — who is trustworthy, who is dangerous, what is happening — partly through gossip.

None of this makes gossip harmless, but it explains why it is so persistent and deeply woven into human life.

Understanding how gossip is used in phrases will help you recognize and use it naturally:

  • Idle gossip — gossip with no serious purpose; pure timewasting chatter. "Pay no attention to idle gossip."
  • Malicious gossip — gossip intended to harm someone's reputation. "She was the victim of malicious gossip spread by a jealous rival."
  • Spread gossip — to pass on rumours to others. "He has a habit of spreading gossip around the office."
  • Gossip column — a section in a newspaper or magazine dedicated to celebrity news, rumours, and personal stories about famous people.
  • The latest gossip — the most recent rumours and personal news. "Tell me the latest gossip — what's been happening while I was away?"
  • A piece of gossip — one specific rumour or story. "She came running in with a juicy piece of gossip."
  • Juicy gossip — gossip that is particularly exciting, scandalous, or interesting. The word juicy here is informal and means "full of interesting detail."

What it isCasual talk about other people's private lives, often unverified
Who it's aboutThird parties — people absent from the conversation
What it involvesSecrets, rumours, personal matters, scandals
Its reliabilityOften uncertain, exaggerated, or distorted
Its toneMostly negative, sometimes neutral, rarely positive
As a personSomeone who habitually spreads such talk

Gossip, in short, is the currency of private social knowledge — information about people's personal lives that circulates informally, behind their backs, in conversations that mix truth with rumour, and are driven more by human curiosity and social bonding than by any need to be accurate or fair.
7007: To gossip means to talk about other people — their personal lives, relationships, problems, secrets, or behavior — usually when those people are not present in the conversation.
What makes it "gossip" and not just regular talk?

Not all talk about other people counts as gossip. The word specifically describes casual, informal conversation where the focus is on personal information about someone — things like who is dating whom, who did something embarrassing, who is having trouble at work, who said something behind someone's back, and so on.

The person being discussed is typically absent. They have not given permission for their personal information to be shared. That's a key part of what makes the word carry a slightly uncomfortable feeling.
Does the information have to be false?

No — this is a common misunderstanding. Gossip does not have to be false or made-up to be gossip. Even true information counts as gossip if it is personal, private, and shared about someone who isn't there. However, gossip very often does involve rumours, exaggerations, or unverified claims, simply because people tend to pass along things they've heard without checking whether they're actually true.

When people gossip, there is often a sense of secrecy or intimacy — a feeling of "just between us." It tends to happen in hushed voices, in small groups, or in private. This creates a kind of social bonding: sharing a secret makes people feel closer to each other. So gossip, while often criticised, also serves a social function — it is a way people connect, build trust within a group, and feel included.

At the same time, gossip can hurt the person being talked about. It can damage their reputation, spread false information, or violate their privacy. This is why the word generally carries a negative or disapproving tone.
The tone and connotation of the word

"Gossip" is not a neutral word. When you say someone is gossiping, you are implying that what they're doing is somewhat petty, trivial, or inappropriate — even if the information is true. You are suggesting they are talking about things that are none of their business, or spending time on idle chatter rather than something meaningful.

That said, in casual, playful speech, people also use it in a lighter, even affectionate way. Phrases like "Let's gossip!" or "Spill the gossip!" treat it as a fun, harmless activity between friends. So the tone depends on context.
How the verb is used in sentences

The verb is almost always used in one of these two patterns:

  • "gossip about someone/something" — This tells you who or what the gossip is about.
    • "They were gossiping about the new manager all morning."
    • "She always gossips about her neighbours."
  • "gossip with someone" — This tells you who the person is gossiping with.
    • "He spent the whole evening gossiping with his coworkers."

Both patterns can be combined:

  • "She was gossiping with her friends about what happened at the party."

The verb is commonly used in the present continuous ("They are gossiping") or past continuous ("We were gossiping"), which reflects the fact that gossip is usually an ongoing activity rather than a single quick action.

It helps to know the boundary:

  • Discussing a news story about a public figure's professional decisions → usually not gossip (it's public information about their public role).
  • Talking about that same person's private romantic life with someone who wasn't there → gossip.
  • Telling a friend that a colleague made a good presentation → not gossip.
  • Telling a friend that the same colleague is apparently going through a divorce → gossip.

The line is: personal life + absent person + informal sharing = gossip.

To gossip is to casually talk about another person's private life, relationships, or behaviour — usually behind their back, sometimes with unverified information, and often with a tone that is judgmental, curious, or entertaining.
7008:
A gossipmonger is a person who loves to collect, spread, and share rumours, secrets, and private information about other people — especially information that is unverified, personal, or potentially damaging to someone's reputation.

The word is made of two parts: gossip (rumour or private talk about others) and monger (a dealer or trader in something). So, literally, a gossipmonger is someone who trades in gossip — they gather it, distribute it, and keep it flowing, much like a merchant keeps goods moving.

Not everyone who gossips is a gossipmonger. The word describes a habitual, enthusiastic, and deliberate spreader of gossip. Here are the key qualities that define one:

1. They actively seek out private information.
A gossipmonger doesn't just accidentally overhear something and mention it once. They hunt for secrets, rumours, and personal details about others. They pay close attention to other people's lives — who is dating whom, who got fired, who is having family trouble — and they treat that information like treasure.

2. They spread information eagerly and widely.
Once they have a piece of gossip, they can't keep it to themselves. They share it with as many people as possible, often with great excitement. The spreading is just as important to them as the collecting.

3. They don't verify what they share.
A gossipmonger rarely checks whether the information is true. They pass it on whether it's fact, half-truth, or pure rumour. Accuracy is not their priority — the thrill of the story is.

4. This is a pattern, not a one-time thing.
This is perhaps the most important point. Everyone gossips occasionally — that's human nature. But a gossipmonger does it constantly and compulsively. It is a defining part of their behaviour, not a rare slip.

5. They often enjoy the drama it creates.
Many gossipmongers are motivated by the feeling of power and importance that comes from being "the one who knows." Sharing a secret makes them feel central, relevant, and interesting.

Gossipmonger is always negative. It is a word of criticism and disapproval. If you call someone a gossipmonger, you are insulting them — you're saying they are untrustworthy, intrusive, and harmful to others. The word implies that the person has a nosy, meddlesome character and little respect for other people's privacy.

No one calls themselves a gossipmonger. It is always a label placed on someone by others.

To make this concrete, here are some everyday situations:

  • Your neighbour constantly asks prying questions about other neighbours, then runs and tells everyone what they found out. They tell people about divorces, financial troubles, and personal conflicts — things that were never meant to be public. That neighbour is a gossipmonger.
  • There's someone at your workplace who always seems to know who is about to get fired, who had an argument with the boss, and who is secretly looking for another job. They whisper this information to everyone and delight in being the person "in the know." That person is a gossipmonger.
  • A character in a novel who spends her days peering through curtains, listening at doors, and then spreading rumours about everyone in the village — she is the classic gossipmonger.

• "Don't tell Adrian anything personal — he's a complete gossipmonger and the whole office will know by Tuesday."
  • "The small town had its share of gossipmongers who turned every minor event into a full-blown scandal."
  • "She had a reputation as a gossipmonger, so people were careful about what they said around her."
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Gossip (noun) — can refer to the information itself ("Did you hear the latest gossip?") or a person who gossips, but it is softer and less harsh than gossipmonger.
  • Gossipmonger — emphasises the deliberate, habitual, and almost professional-level nature of the spreading. It is stronger and more condemning.
  • Rumormonger — nearly identical in meaning; just uses "rumor" instead of "gossip." Both describe the same type of person.
  • Busybody — a person who meddles in others' affairs, but the focus is on interfering, not necessarily on spreading information.
  • Tattletale — used mostly for children; refers to someone who tells on others, usually to an authority figure.
The Social Harm a Gossipmonger Causes

It is worth understanding why this word carries such a negative charge. A gossipmonger can genuinely hurt people. When false or private information is spread widely:

  • Reputations can be damaged unfairly.
  • Friendships and relationships can be broken.
  • People can lose jobs or social standing.
  • The victim can feel humiliated, betrayed, and unsafe.

This is why a gossipmonger is not seen as merely annoying — they are seen as a genuinely harmful presence in a community.

A gossipmonger is someone who makes a habit — almost a hobby — of collecting and spreading rumours, secrets, and private information about others, usually without caring whether it's true or whether it hurts anyone. The word is always used as a criticism, pointing to someone who is nosy, untrustworthy, and damaging to the social fabric around them. The stronger and more deliberate the behaviour, the more fitting the label.
7009: "Gothic" is a word that wears many different hats depending on the context — it can describe an ancient people, a style of buildings, a type of storytelling, a font, and even a modern fashion subculture. But here is the beautiful part: almost all of these meanings share the same emotional core — something that feels dark, grand, mysterious, and tied to the medieval past. Once you understand that thread, the word becomes very easy to navigate.
1. Gothic — Relating to the Ancient Goths (Historical)

In its most literal and oldest sense, "gothic" simply means relating to the Goths — a group of Germanic tribes (the Visigoths and Ostrogoths) who lived in Europe roughly between the 3rd and 6th centuries AD and famously played a large role in the collapse of the Western Roman Empire.

When used in this sense, the word is almost always capitalized: Gothic tribes, Gothic kings, Gothic migrations. This meaning is mostly confined to history books and academic writing, so you're unlikely to encounter it in everyday conversation.
2. Gothic Architecture — The Grand, Soaring Style of Medieval Cathedrals

This is probably the most well-known and important meaning of the word.

Gothic architecture is a style of building that originated in France in the 12th century and spread across Europe throughout the Middle Ages. When you see an enormous medieval cathedral with dramatic, towering walls, enormous stained-glass windows flooding the interior with coloured light, and spires reaching sharply into the sky — that is Gothic architecture.

The defining features you'll recognize:

  • Pointed arches — instead of the older rounded Roman arches, Gothic arches come to a sharp point at the top. This is perhaps the single most recognizable feature of the style.
  • Ribbed vaults — the ceilings are supported by a network of stone ribs, which allow the building to soar higher than ever before.
  • Flying buttresses — these are the external stone arms that jut out from the sides of a cathedral wall. They look almost like a skeleton on the outside of the building. Their job is to carry the weight of the walls and roof outward and downward, which frees up the walls themselves to be thinner and full of windows instead of solid stone.
  • Large stained-glass windows — because the flying buttresses carry the structural load, the walls no longer need to be thick and solid. This allowed architects to fill them with enormous windows of coloured glass depicting religious stories.
  • Height and verticality — everything in Gothic architecture reaches upward. The effect is intentional: it was meant to fill the worshipper with a sense of awe, smallness, and the presence of God.
  • Gargoyles and decorative carvings — grotesque stone creatures, intricate floral patterns, and detailed sculptures adorn the exterior.

Famous examples of Gothic architecture include the Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, Chartres Cathedral, Westminster Abbey in London, and the Cologne Cathedral in Germany. When people call something "gothic-looking," they often mean it has this dark, grand, medieval, stone-and-spire quality.
3. Gothic Literature — Dark, Mysterious, and Spine-Chilling Stories

Inspired directly by the atmosphere of those gloomy, magnificent medieval buildings, a literary genre emerged in the 18th century that we call Gothic fiction or Gothic literature.

Gothic literature deals in darkness — not just physical darkness, but psychological and emotional darkness too. Think of it as the ancestor of both the horror and psychological thriller genres. It creates a specific mood: dread, mystery, eeriness, and suspense, often set against crumbling old buildings and isolated landscapes.

The key ingredients of Gothic fiction include:

  • Dark, atmospheric settings — decrepit castles, crumbling mansions, foggy moors, graveyards, dungeons. The setting is never cheerful or ordinary; it is almost a character in itself.
  • A sense of mystery or dread — something unknown, threatening, or supernatural lurks beneath the surface.
  • The supernatural — ghosts, monsters, vampires, curses, and unexplained phenomena are common.
  • Psychological terror — the horror is often as much internal (inside a character's mind) as it is external.
  • Decay and death — themes of mortality, rot, ruin, and the past haunting the present run through the genre.
  • Intense emotion — passion, obsession, grief, guilt, and madness.

Famous examples: Dracula by Bram Stoker, Frankenstein by Mary Shelley, Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë, The Castle of Otranto by Horace Walpole (the very first Gothic novel), and Rebecca by Daphne du Maurier. Films like Interview with the Vampire, Crimson Peak, and countless haunted-house movies belong to this tradition.

There is also a specifically American branch called Southern Gothic, which takes Gothic elements and places them in the American South — focusing on racial trauma, social decay, eccentricity, and moral darkness. Flannery O'Connor and William Faulkner are the most celebrated writers in this tradition.

When you call a film, novel, or TV show "gothic," you mean it has this dark, mysterious, brooding, and often supernatural atmosphere.
4. Gothic Typeface — The Old, Ornate Style of Writing

You have almost certainly seen Gothic lettering without knowing what to call it. It is the style of writing that looks ancient, angular, heavily decorated, and almost difficult to read — the kind you see on old church documents, university diplomas, the masthead of old newspapers like The New York Times, medieval manuscripts, and the labels of certain beer brands (like Budweiser).

This style is also called blackletter or Old English. It was the dominant style of writing in Western Europe during the Middle Ages before the cleaner, rounder typefaces we use today took over during the Renaissance.

When something is written in "gothic font," it has this old, ornate, somewhat heavy and dramatic quality.

(Note: In American typographical terminology, "gothic" can also — confusingly — refer to simple, plain sans-serif typefaces. But this usage is mostly technical and confined to the field of typography.)
5. Gothic Subculture — A Modern Aesthetic and Lifestyle

From the late 1970s onward, a subculture emerged from post-punk music that took the word "gothic" and applied it to a particular aesthetic and way of life. This is what people usually mean when they call a person or fashion style "gothic" or "goth."

The Gothic subculture is characterized by:

  • Dark clothing — predominantly black, often with lace, leather, velvet, or Victorian-inspired elements.
  • Dark makeup — black eyeliner, pale foundation, dark or black lipstick.
  • Interest in the macabre and death — not necessarily in a morbid or unhealthy way, but as an acceptance and even aesthetic appreciation of darkness, mortality, and things that mainstream culture tends to avoid.
  • Gothic and darkwave music — bands like The Cure, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Joy Division, Bauhaus, and Type O Negative are central to this musical tradition.
  • A sensibility, not just a look — many people who identify with the goth subculture see it as a way of engaging with the darker, more melancholic, and more complex sides of human experience.

When you say someone "looks gothic" or "dresses in a gothic style," you are referring to this dark, brooding, often black-clad aesthetic.
6. Gothic Art — The Visual Art of the Middle Ages

Alongside Gothic architecture, there is also Gothic art — a term used for the painting, sculpture, and manuscript illumination produced in Europe roughly from the 12th to the 16th century. Early Gothic paintings often featured flat, two-dimensional figures on gold backgrounds with religious themes. Over time, Gothic art became progressively more realistic, with greater attention to human emotion, drapery, and natural detail. Think of the intricate stone carvings on the exterior of a cathedral, or the glowing religious paintings of artists like Giotto — these fall under the Gothic art tradition.

With the exception of the purely historical meaning (the Goths as a people), every other use of "gothic" evokes a similar emotional world: something that is dark, grand, mysterious, and rooted in the medieval past.

Gothic architecture is imposing and full of shadows and spiritual gravity. Gothic literature is atmospheric, eerie, and obsessed with darkness and death. Gothic typeface looks ancient and heavy. The Gothic subculture embraces darkness as beauty. Gothic art is solemn and devotional.

So if you ever encounter the word "gothic" and you're unsure what it means precisely, ask yourself: is this about medieval grandeur? Is it dark and atmospheric? Is it mysterious and a little bit eerie? If the answer is yes, you are on the right track.

• "The cathedral had gothic arches." → architectural style
  • "The film had a gothic atmosphere — all fog, crumbling mansions, and dread." → literary/cinematic mood
  • "She wore all black and dark makeup — very gothic." → subculture aesthetic
  • "The diploma was printed in a gothic font." → typeface
  • "Gothic tribes invaded Rome." → historical (relating to the Goths as a people; usually capitalized)
7010: Gouache is a type of paint — and also the name for a painting made using that paint.

Gouache is a water-based paint, meaning you thin it with water (not oil or chemicals) and you clean your brushes with plain water. In that sense, it is a close cousin of watercolor.

But here is the single most important thing that sets gouache apart from watercolor: gouache is opaque. "Opaque" means light cannot pass through it — you cannot see through a layer of gouache the way you can see through a layer of watercolor. When you paint with gouache, the color sits on the surface as a solid, dense layer. It covers whatever is underneath it.

Watercolor, by contrast, is transparent — it is like tinted glass. You can see the white of the paper shining through it, which gives watercolor its luminous, delicate look. Gouache has no such luminosity; instead, it gives you flat, bold, solid color. Think of the difference between a stained-glass window (transparent — like watercolor) and a painted wall (opaque — like gouache).
What gouache looks and feels like

• Matte finish. When dry, gouache has a flat, non-shiny surface. It does not gleam the way oil paint or acrylic can.
  • Velvety texture. The dried surface has a slightly chalky, soft quality that many artists love.
  • Thick and creamy. Straight from the tube or pan, gouache is quite thick. Artists add water to thin it to whatever consistency they need.
One very important quirk: it dries lighter

When gouache is wet, it looks darker and more saturated. When it dries, it becomes noticeably lighter and slightly chalky. This is one of the first things any gouache user discovers and must learn to account for. Experienced gouache artists mentally compensate by mixing colors a little darker than they want the final result to be.
A big practical advantage: you can paint light over dark

Because gouache is opaque, you can paint a bright white or light yellow directly over a dark blue or black background, and it will show up perfectly. This is impossible with transparent watercolor — with watercolor, once you paint dark, that area stays dark; you can only go darker. Gouache reverses this freedom. You can go from dark to light at any point.

This is why gouache is popular for illustration, especially when an artist wants crisp highlights, bright colors on dark paper, or bold graphic shapes.
It stays water-soluble even after drying

Unlike acrylic paint, which becomes plastic and permanent when dry, gouache stays soluble in water permanently. This means even a painting that dried weeks ago can be accidentally damaged if it gets wet — a drop of water on a finished gouache painting can dissolve and smear the surface. It also means you can reactivate dried paint on your palette simply by adding water, which reduces waste.
What surfaces is it used on?

Gouache is most commonly used on paper — especially thick, textured paper or illustration board. It can also be used on cardboard. It does not work well on canvas (which is better suited for oil or acrylic), because canvas flexes and can cause dried gouache to crack. Unlike watercolor, gouache can be used beautifully on toned or dark-colored paper, because of its opacity.
Who uses gouache and for what?

• Illustrators — gouache has been one of the most popular tools in book illustration and editorial illustration for over a century, because it produces clean, flat colors that reproduce well in print.
  • Graphic designers (historically, before computers) — gouache was the go-to medium for creating artwork that needed solid, predictable, reproducible colors.
  • Fine artists — many painters use gouache for sketching, for finished artworks, or for adding opaque highlights on top of a watercolor base.
  • Concept artists and animators — it was widely used in pre-digital animation and concept art for film and games.
The second meaning: a gouache as a painting

"A gouache" (with an indefinite article) also refers to a finished painting made using gouache paint — the same way "a watercolor" means a painting done in watercolor. So a museum label might read: "Untitled, 1947, gouache on paper." Here, the word tells you both the medium used and, by implication, the style and look of the piece.

Gouache
BaseWater
OpacityFully opaque
Finish when dryFlat/matte
DriesLighter than when wet
Re-soluble in water?Yes, always
Best surfacePaper, board
Main useIllustration, fine art, design

In short: gouache is the paint you choose when you want solid, opaque, matte color that you can apply with water, on paper, in any order — dark over light or light over dark. It sits right between watercolor (transparent, delicate) and acrylic (opaque, permanent), borrowing convenience from one and boldness from the other.
7011: Before jumping into the meanings, it helps to picture the central idea behind the word. Think of a sharp, scooping action — something that digs into a surface and removes material from it, leaving a hollow, carved-out mark. That image of "digging in and scooping out" is the heart of the word "gouge," and it runs through all its meanings.

A gouge is a specific type of hand tool used in woodworking, sculpting, and carpentry. It looks similar to a chisel, but unlike a chisel — which has a flat blade — a gouge has a curved, hollow blade, shaped like a small scoop or the inside of a spoon.

When a craftsman presses a gouge into wood (or stone or similar materials) and pushes it forward, it doesn't just cut a straight line. It scoops out a curved groove or channel, removing a bit of the material. This makes it ideal for carving curved shapes, hollowing out surfaces, making decorative patterns in wood, or shaping the inside of a wooden bowl.

Different gouges have differently sized and shaped blades — some have a very shallow curve, almost flat; others have a deep U-shape, like a tiny tunnel. Woodcarvers and sculptors might own a whole set of them in various shapes.

The sculptor used a gouge to hollow out the eye sockets on the wooden mask.
Meaning 2: A Deep Cut, Groove, or Hole in a Surface

This is the most commonly encountered meaning in everyday life. A gouge is a mark, hole, or channel left in a surface when something hard, sharp, or forceful digs into it — the way the tool above digs into wood.

The key quality of a gouge (as a mark) is depth and removal. It's not a thin scratch on the surface. It's a place where material has actually been scooped out or torn away, leaving a noticeable dent, groove, or cavity. The wound in the surface is deeper and wider than a scratch.

Where you might encounter this meaning:

  • A wooden floor might have a gouge in it where a heavy piece of furniture was dragged across it, tearing out a chunk of the wood.
  • A car's metal panel might have a deep gouge from where it scraped against something sharp.
  • A road or pavement might show a gouge where heavy construction machinery ran over it.
  • A rock face or cliff might have a gouge carved into it by a glacier over thousands of years.
  • A cricket pitch or a baseball field might develop a gouge after repeated use.

Essentially, anytime you see a surface that looks like something took a bite out of it — not just a thin line, but a small hollow or channel — that's a gouge.

There was a long, ugly gouge in the dining table where the child had dragged a toy car.
Meaning 3: An Act of Overcharging or Swindling (Informal)

In informal English, a gouge can refer to an instance of being charged an unfairly or outrageously high price, or being cheated or exploited financially, especially when the person being charged has little choice in the matter.

When people use this meaning, they're saying the seller "dug into" their wallet and took out far more than was fair — borrowing the same idea of digging in and taking out. It often implies that the seller is deliberately taking advantage of someone's desperation, lack of alternatives, or a shortage of a product.

You'll notice this meaning used frequently:

  • During a natural disaster, when some shops charge five times the normal price for bottled water. People call this a price gouge (the related act is called "price gouging").
  • When a mechanic charges $800 for a repair that should cost $200 — calling it a gouge means they felt cheated.
  • A tourist trap restaurant in a popular city charging $30 for a plain sandwich might be called a gouge.

Buying a $15 bottle of water at the airport? That's a total gouge.

It's worth seeing the connection clearly:

The tool (meaning 1) performs a physical scooping action — it digs in and removes something. The mark it leaves (meaning 2) is the result of that action — a hole or groove in something. The financial overcharging (meaning 3) borrows this image metaphorically — someone is digging into your money and scooping out more than they deserve.

All three share that central idea: something sharp and aggressive going into something and taking out more than it should.

As a physical tool: A curved chisel used to scoop out grooves in wood or stone.

As a mark on a surface: A deep cut or hollow where material has been scooped out or torn away; more than a scratch — an actual chunk or channel missing from the surface.

As an informal act: An instance of being charged an unfairly high price; being financially exploited, especially when you're in a position of disadvantage.
7012: Gouge means to dig into or scoop out material by force, or to unfairly take something from someone (usually money). Both meanings share a common thread: something is being forcefully extracted — either from a surface or from a person's pocket.
Meaning 1: To Dig, Scoop, or Cut Into a Surface

When you gouge something, you are not making a neat, clean cut. You are digging into a surface with force and tearing out a piece of it, leaving behind a deep groove, channel, or hollow. The result is always a visible wound on the surface — a rough, sunken mark.

Think of it this way: a knife slices, a needle pricks, but a gouge rips out a chunk. It's aggressive, and the damage it leaves is hard to miss.

Examples:

  • "He dropped his keys on the wooden floor, and they gouged a deep scratch into it." (The keys dug in and tore out a groove.)
  • "The bulldozer gouged a trench across the muddy field." (It scooped out a long channel of earth by force.)
  • "A sharp rock gouged the side of my car." (It dug in and left a deep, ugly mark.)

The Phrase: "Gouge Out"

You will very often see gouge paired with "out" — gouge out. This means to fully dig something out of a surface, removing it completely.

  • "The sculptor gouged out the excess wood to reveal the shape beneath."
  • "The river, over thousands of years, gouged out a canyon from the rock."
  • In dramatic or violent language, people say things like "gouge out someone's eyes", meaning to dig them out forcefully. This is a vivid, brutal expression you'll encounter in fiction or strong speech.

The word "out" signals that the material is not just dug into, but fully removed.

The Feeling of the Word

Gouge always carries a sense of roughness and damage. It is never delicate. When you hear that something has been gouged, you picture an ugly, ragged hole or channel — not a tidy cut. The word itself sounds violent: even its pronunciation feels sharp and aggressive.
Meaning 2: To Cheat Someone by Overcharging Them

The second major meaning of gouge is financial. To gouge someone means to charge them an outrageously unfair, excessive price — to exploit them and take far more money than is reasonable or honest.

This meaning is a metaphor rooted in the first: just as physical gouging rips material out of a surface, financial gouging rips money out of someone's pocket against their will (or at least against their best interests).

Examples:

  • "The hotel gouged tourists by charging $800 a night for a basic room."
  • "After the hurricane, some fuel stations gouged desperate customers, selling gas at five times the normal price."
  • "I felt completely gouged after paying $30 for a sandwich at the airport."

"Price Gouging" — A Very Common Phrase

You will frequently encounter the compound phrase price gouging. This refers to the practice of sellers dramatically raising prices during a crisis, emergency, or shortage — when people are vulnerable and have few other options. Because victims of a disaster need food, water, or medicine urgently, they cannot say no, and dishonest sellers exploit this. Price gouging is widely considered unethical and is illegal in many places.

  • "After the flood, several hardware stores were accused of price gouging, selling generators at triple their normal cost."

The reason "gouge" is used here, rather than just "overcharge," is because gouge implies exploitation and aggression — you are not just charging more, you are ripping into someone's finances, taking far more than they should ever have had to give.
How Gouge Differs From Similar Words

Understanding a word also means knowing how it sits alongside words that seem similar.

Gouge vs. Cut: A cut is neutral — it can be clean, precise, and controlled. A gouge is always rough, deep, and associated with damage.

Gouge vs. Scratch: A scratch is superficial, barely breaking the surface. A gouge goes deep, often removing material entirely. If a scratch is a paper cut, a gouge is a chunk taken out of your arm.

Gouge vs. Carve: Carving is intentional and skilled — you carve a sculpture or carve a turkey. Gouging is destructive, even when deliberate. You would not say an artist "gouged" a beautiful statue (unless they were roughing it out violently or you were being critical).

Gouge vs. Overcharge: Overcharging sounds like a mistake or a business decision. Gouging carries moral weight — it means taking advantage of someone, exploiting their vulnerability. It's a much stronger accusation.
Summary: One Word, One Big Idea

Whether physical or financial, gouge always means the same thing at its core:

To forcefully dig in and take out more than you should, leaving damage behind.

In the physical world, it leaves a rough hole or groove in a surface.
In the human world, it leaves someone feeling ripped off, exploited, and robbed.

That is the word gouge — sharp, aggressive, and always a little bit unfair.
7013:
Before understanding the full phrase, you need to know what gouge means on its own.

A gouge (noun) is a special tool that looks like a chisel but has a curved or hollow blade. It is used in woodworking to scoop, carve, or hollow out material. Because of the way this tool works — digging into something and ripping material away — the word "gouge" became a verb meaning to cut, dig, or scoop into something forcefully, often leaving a deep mark, groove, or hole behind.

The action of gouging is never gentle. It is rough, forceful, and usually leaves damage behind.

When you add "out" to "gouge," it becomes a phrasal verb — and that little word "out" is very important. It shifts the meaning from just cutting into something to removing something entirely from within it. The "out" tells you that whatever was inside is now gone — dug, scooped, or torn away completely.

Think of it like the difference between:

  • "Dig" → you are making a hole
  • "Dig out" → you are removing something that was buried inside

The same logic applies to "gouge out."

To gouge out means to forcefully dig, scoop, carve, or tear something out of a surface or a body, leaving a hollow, groove, or empty space behind.

The action is always:

  • Forceful — it takes effort and pressure
  • Rough — it is not precise or careful
  • Destructive — it damages the surface or object
  • Removes material — something is taken away, not just marked
The Three Main Ways It Is Used

1. Literally — Removing Something From a Surface

This is when something physically digs into a hard surface and removes a chunk of material, leaving a pit, groove, or hollow behind.

Examples:

  • "The bulldozer gouged out a huge section of the earth to lay the foundation."
  • "A falling rock gouged out a deep hole in the roof of the car."
  • "He used a knife to gouge out the rotten part of the wooden door."
  • "The bullet gouged out a chunk of plaster from the wall."

In all of these, you can picture something being forcefully dug into, with a piece being ripped away, leaving a visible wound or hole in the surface.

2. Literally — Removing Eyes (The Most Famous Use)

One of the most well-known and dramatic uses of "gouge out" is with eyes. To gouge out someone's eyes means to violently remove the eyeballs from their sockets, often with a finger, tool, or weapon.

This usage appears frequently in:

  • Classic literature and mythology (Oedipus gouged out his own eyes as punishment in the ancient Greek tragedy)
  • Fantasy and horror fiction (villains threatening enemies this way)
  • War and historical accounts
  • Everyday expressions (often used hyperbolically to show extreme anger)

Examples:

  • "In the story, the soldier threatened to gouge out the prisoner's eyes."
  • "I was so angry I could have gouged his eyes out!" (hyperbole — not meant literally)
  • "The surgeon had to carefully gouge out the damaged tissue around the eye."

This use is graphic and violent in nature, which is why it appears so often in dramatic storytelling.

3. Literally — Natural Forces Carving Into the Earth

Nature also "gouges out" things over long periods of time. Glaciers, rivers, wind, and water can slowly but powerfully dig into rock and earth, hollowing out landscapes.

Examples:

  • "Over millions of years, the Colorado River gouged out the Grand Canyon."
  • "The glacier gouged out a long, deep valley as it moved slowly across the land."
  • "Wind and water have gouged out caves in the cliffside."

Here, the meaning is the same — something is forcefully and repeatedly digging into a surface, removing material, and leaving a hollow space — but the agent is a natural force rather than a person or tool.

"Gouge out" is a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the thing being gouged) can go either:

Between the two words:

  • "He gouged out a piece of wood." ✅
  • "She gouged out his eyes." ✅

Or after both words:

  • "He gouged a piece of wood out." ✅
  • "She gouged his eyes out." ✅

However, if you use a pronoun (like it or them), it must go between the two words:

  • "She gouged them out." ✅
  • "She gouged out them." ❌ — This is grammatically wrong.
The Feeling and Tone of the Phrase

"Gouge out" carries a very specific emotional weight. It almost always suggests:

  • Violence or force — nothing about this phrase is soft or gentle
  • Irreversibility — what has been gouged out cannot easily be put back
  • Destruction — the surface or object that was gouged is damaged or changed permanently
  • Rawness — the image it creates is visceral and physical

Because of these qualities, writers use it deliberately when they want the reader to feel the brutality or power of an action. It is a much stronger and more vivid phrase than softer alternatives like "remove," "take out," or "scoop."

Word/PhraseHow it differs from "gouge out"
Scoop outGentler; suggests a smooth, curved removal (like with a spoon)
Hollow outFocuses on creating an empty space; less violent
Dig outMore general; does not imply the same roughness
Carve outImplies skill and intention; not destructive
Tear outEmphasizes tearing/ripping rather than scooping
ExtractVery formal and clinical; no sense of violence
Pluck outUsually for small things like feathers or eyes; quick action

"Gouge out" sits in a unique spot — it implies more force than "scoop" or "carve," is more specific than "dig," and is more physical and raw than "extract."

The word "gouge" alone (without "out") can also mean to cheat someone by charging them an unfairly high price. For example: "That mechanic gouged me — he charged three times the normal price."

However, "gouge out" is almost never used in this financial sense. If you see "gouge out," it is nearly always the physical meaning — digging, scooping, or tearing something away.

"Gouge out" means to forcefully dig, scoop, or tear something out of a surface or body, leaving a hole or hollow behind. The action is rough, powerful, and destructive. It is used when:

  • A tool, person, or force digs material out of a surface (wood, earth, a wall)
  • Eyes or body parts are violently removed
  • Natural forces (rivers, glaciers) carve hollows into the earth over time

The phrase always suggests force, damage, and removal — and it paints a vivid, raw picture in the reader's mind.
7014: Goulash is a word with two distinct meanings — one very specific, one more general.
Meaning 1: A hearty meat stew (the main meaning)

A goulash is a thick, rich stew — a slow-cooked dish made primarily with chunks of beef (though pork or lamb can be used too), onions, and large amounts of paprika, which is a spice made from dried red peppers. This spice is the soul of goulash: it gives the dish its deep red-orange color, its smoky warmth, and its slightly sweet, mildly spicy flavor.

Other common ingredients include potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, tomatoes, and garlic, all simmered together in a savory broth until everything becomes tender and the flavors meld into one deeply satisfying whole. The result is thick — almost saucy — and warming, the kind of food people eat in cold weather.

Goulash is considered the national dish of Hungary, where it has been cooked for centuries. It is sometimes served over egg noodles or bread. When eaten in a thinner, more soup-like form, it is called goulash soup (known in Hungarian as gulyásleves), though the word "goulash" in English typically refers to the thicker stew version. The dish has spread across Central and Eastern Europe, so you'll find variations in countries like Austria, Czech Republic, Poland, and Germany — each with slight differences in ingredients or preparation, but all recognizable as goulash.

In American English, a simplified home-cooking version of goulash also exists — often made with ground beef, pasta (like macaroni), tomato sauce, and mild spices. This is quite different from the Hungarian original but goes by the same name, usually called American goulash or American chop suey to distinguish it.

In informal everyday speech, particularly in American English, goulash is also used figuratively to describe a messy mix of unrelated or poorly organized things — similar to words like "hodgepodge," "mishmash," or "jumble."

For example:

  • "The new policy document is a goulash of old rules, new ideas, and contradictory instructions."
  • "His speech was a complete goulash — no clear argument, just random thoughts thrown together."

This figurative meaning draws directly from the dish: just as goulash contains many ingredients thrown into one pot, this sense of the word describes things that feel thrown together without clear order or purpose. This usage is casual and informal — you'd say it in conversation or light writing, not in formal documents.

Think of goulash as "a thick Hungarian beef stew, red from paprika" for its literal meaning, and "a messy mix of things" for its figurative one. Both meanings share the same image: many things cooked or thrown together into one pot.
7015:
A gourd is a fruit that grows on a vine. It belongs to the same plant family as cucumbers, pumpkins, melons, and squash — so it is a close cousin of all of these. In fact, pumpkins and squashes are themselves a type of gourd, though we rarely call them that in everyday speech.

What sets gourds apart from their cousins is their tough, hard outer shell. While a cucumber is soft and you eat the whole thing, a gourd has a thick, rigid skin that can become almost wood-like when the fruit dries out. This hardness is the defining quality that makes gourds so special and so useful throughout human history.

Gourds come in a surprising variety of shapes and sizes. Some are round like a ball. Some look like a bottle — wide and round at the bottom, with a long narrow neck rising up (this is the classic "bottle gourd" shape that most people picture when they hear the word). Some are long and curved like a snake. Some are small and bumpy and look almost alien.

Their colours vary too — green, yellow, orange, cream, white, or mottled with patches of different colours. The skin is usually smooth or slightly ridged, and it feels firm and solid to the touch.

This is an important thing to understand: a gourd has two very different phases, and the word "gourd" can refer to either one.

1. The fresh, living fruit
When a gourd is freshly harvested from the vine, it is moist inside, with flesh and seeds, just like any other fruit or vegetable. At this stage, many gourds are eaten as food. In Indian cooking, for example, the bottle gourd (lauki or dudhi), the bitter gourd (karela), the ridge gourd (turai), and the snake gourd are all very common vegetables that people cook and eat.

2. The dried shell
When a gourd is left to dry out — either on the vine or after harvesting — the moisture inside evaporates over weeks or months. What remains is a hollow, dry, extremely hard shell. This dried gourd shell is lightweight but surprisingly strong and durable. It is this form of the gourd that humans have found endlessly useful for thousands of years.
What people do with gourds (especially dried ones)

The dried gourd shell is essentially a ready-made container. Because of this, people around the world have used gourds in countless practical and creative ways:

As containers and vessels: Before plastic bottles, metal cans, or glass jars existed, dried gourds served as water flasks, storage jars, bowls, cups, and ladles. A bottle-shaped gourd, for instance, made a perfect natural canteen — you simply dry it out, cut a small opening at the narrow neck, and you have a vessel that can hold water or grain. This use goes back thousands of years across Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

As musical instruments: Because a dried gourd is hollow and hard, it resonates beautifully when struck or shaken. Gourds are used to make percussion instruments (like maracas, where seeds or small stones are placed inside a dried gourd and shaken), string instruments (the gourd acts as the resonating chamber, like the body of a guitar), and wind instruments. The West African kora, a 21-string instrument, uses a large dried gourd as its sound box. Instruments using gourds are found in music traditions across Africa, Latin America, South Asia, and beyond.

As decoration: Smaller, ornamental gourds with interesting shapes and bright colours are grown purely to look beautiful. In many parts of the world, a bowl of colourful decorative gourds is a classic symbol of autumn and harvest time. You might see them displayed in homes, at markets, or on dining tables in the fall.

As utensils and tools: Gourds have been carved and shaped into spoons, ladles, scoops, and even birdhouses. Some cultures use them as pipes. Indigenous and tribal communities across the world have developed elaborate traditions of gourd-carving and decorating, turning them into art.

You may sometimes hear the word calabash used almost interchangeably with "gourd." A calabash is specifically the bottle gourd (Lagenaria siceraria) — the classic long-necked variety — and also refers to the dried shell of that particular gourd.
